newsitem.title: USA: Dominican smuggling rings growing problem for U.S.
newsitem.headline: Dominican smuggling rings growing problem for U.S.

text.p: Growing numbers of poor people from the Dominican Republic are trying to reach the United States illegally by paying smuggling gangs to run them from their homeland to Puerto Rico in hazardous night-time sea crossings, U.S. Coast Guard officials say.
The Dominican migrants now outnumber Cubans and Haitians, previously prime concerns for U.S. immigration and law enforcement officials watching the Caribbean Sea.

"Human smuggling is big business," U.S. Coast Guard Lt. Cdr. Marcus Woodring told Reuters. He said the gangs were highly organised. "They take on human cargoes and they appear to have little regard for human life."

The trip for the Dominicans entails a journey of up 18 hours across the Mona Passage, infamous for its treacherous waters. The channel separates the Dominican Republic from Puerto Rico, which as a U.S. Commonwealth gains the illegal immigrants a foothold from which the lucky ones can carry on to mainland United States.

The boats, known as "Yolas", usually leave from Miches on the north coast or La Romana in the south under cover of darkness, Woodring said. The long, narrow boats equipped with outboard motors travel with a captain, two "enforcers" and up to 40 or 50 passengers.
Sometimes boards are removed to make the vessel even lower in the water to avoid radar detection. They rarely have radar, flares or lifejackets but they often carry extra fuel.
"These boats are highly dangerous," Woodring said.
Last week a boat believed to be a smuggling yola sank in the channel when a fire broke out. About 40 people were lost, according to Dominican authorities.

The migrants are usually fairly well-dressed so they can blend in with Puerto Ricans when they land, Woodring said. They reach the beach, scramble up and are usually met -- often piling into cars and buses.
It is not just Dominicans, he said. "We've caught Chinese, Indians, Bangladeshis and Cubans."

The Chinese can pay up to $20,000 for a trip from Asia to New York via the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico, Woodring said. Sometimes they are committed to indentured labour, working as virtual slaves in New York to pay off the debt.
The drug trade is also linked. About 28 per cent of the cocaine coming into the United States arrives via Puerto Rico. So far in 1996, 154 metric tons have been seized.
Some Dominicans pay for the trip with drugs. Others are forced to act as couriers, government sources said.

In previous years U.S. authorities have faced waves of Cuban and Haitian refugees and migrants. This year the Coast Guard has rescued 687 Haitians at sea, down from nearly 2,000 in 1995. The number of Cubans has dropped to 316 from 626.
The number of Dominicans the Coast Guard picked up at sea is 4,162 so far this year, just under the total for 1995.

There are signs that since U.S. policy changes in May 1995, which meant Cubans could be repatriated to the communist-ruled island, the phenomenon of individual "rafters" appears to have given way to organised smuggling rings too, Woodring said.
